title: Julian Calendar
intro: The Julian calendar was introduced in ancient Rome and uses a solar year divided into twelve months. It is similar to the Gregorian calendar but uses a simpler leap-year rule, so the two systems slowly drift apart.
summary: Twelve months. A day is added to February every fourth year, giving 365 days in a common year and 366 in a leap year.
origin: Julius Caesar introduced the Julian reform from 45 BCE. Many communities later switched to the Gregorian calendar, while some religious traditions still use Julian dates.
structure: The month names and ordinary month lengths look familiar. The distinguishing rule is simple: each year divisible by four is a leap year, including century years.
diagram_caption: FEBRUARY IS 29 DAYS EVERY FOURTH YEAR
pattern_note: The Julian calendar's average year is 365.25 days. That is a little longer than the tropical solar year, so the calendar's dates shift against the seasons over many centuries.
history: Julius Caesar's reform replaced an earlier Roman calendar. Leap-day practice in the first decades was not perfectly regular; the software uses the consistent proleptic Julian rule, not early administrative irregularities.
example: During 1900-2099, 1 January on the Julian calendar corresponds to 14 January on the Gregorian calendar: the Julian date is thirteen days behind for the same day.
limits: This is the mathematical Julian calendar extended consistently into other eras. It does not reconstruct the irregular pre-Augustan application of leap years or each region's later calendar changeover.
